blurb: Every repo from the 16 November issue, with what each does and the setup steps from its own README.
intro: Issue #49 had six repos and no AI skills, and this page covers all six. Most are for developers who work with coding agents. If you build for the web, start with Chrome DevTools for agents: one block of config and your agent can debug in a real browser. If you are curious about letting AI use your phone, Pinky has a demo mode you can try first.

items.name: Pinky
items.cost: Free and open source (Apache-2.0), no account needed
items.works_with: Any MCP agent, including Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex and Cursor
items.short: Lets an AI agent use your real iPhone or Android phone while you watch, approve risky taps and take over at any time.
items.what: Pinky is a desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux that lets an agent operate a real phone over MCP. You watch in Pinky's window, approve risky steps such as payments, and can take over whenever you like. It can also run tasks by itself with a model you pick, from your computer or from Pinky's app on the phone.
items.who: People who want an agent to do tasks on their phone and still keep control of what it taps. The project calls itself pre-alpha, so if you need something proven and stable, wait.
needs: macOS 13 or later, Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit), or 64-bit Linux with Ubuntu 20.04, Debian 11 or newer and GTK 3
An Android phone on Android 10 to 17, or an iPhone or iPad on iOS 17.4 or later, plus a USB cable
USB debugging turned on, for Android
Any agent that can use MCP servers

steps.title: Install the app
steps.text: Download it from the latest release on GitHub. On a Mac you can use Homebrew instead.

steps.title: Connect your phone
steps.text: Open Pinky and choose Add phone. For Android, turn on USB debugging, plug the phone in and tap Allow when it asks. Pinky shows steps for your phone's brand and a Checkup for anything missing.

steps.title: Add Pinky to your agent
steps.text: In Pinky, open Settings › Agents and click Connect next to your agent. Pinky adds itself to the agent's MCP servers and installs its agent guide.

steps.title: Or add it by hand in Claude Code
steps.text: The command is `pinkyctl`, not `pinky`.
steps.code: claude mcp add --scope user pinky -- pinkyctl mcp

steps.title: Try it without a phone
steps.text: Quit Pinky and start it with two scripted demo phones. This is the Linux command; the README gives the Mac and Windows versions too.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Open Messages on my phone and tell Sam I'm running late.

watch: The agent can see and tap your phone's screen. Payments wait for your click by default. You can make sends, deletions, installs and more wait too in Settings › Safety.
Banking, wallet and password manager apps are hidden from agents by default, and agents cannot type into password or one-time-code fields.
It sends anonymous usage statistics and crash reports. Turn them off in Settings › Privacy or with `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`.
The Windows installer is not signed yet, so SmartScreen may warn you.
For iPhones it may download Apple's developer disk image from a third-party mirror, only if you ask it to.
The project says it is pre-alpha, and some features still wait for a person to try them.

items.name: Kiri
items.works_with: The docker CLI, Docker Compose and buildx
items.short: A small, fast container runtime in Rust that runs your Docker images and works with the docker CLI and Compose you already use.
items.what: Kiri replaces Docker Desktop and OrbStack. It runs containers in one small Linux VM, or straight on the kernel on Linux, and speaks the Docker Engine API, so your existing tools keep working. It also gives you local domains with HTTPS, a one-command Kubernetes cluster, Linux machines and a native window.
items.who: Developers who run containers every day and find Docker Desktop heavy. If you depend on Docker's own build endpoints, note that the built-in builder is still on the roadmap.
needs: macOS 14 or later (Apple silicon or Intel), Windows 10 or 11 with WSL 2, or Linux with .deb or .rpm packages
The docker CLI if you want to use docker commands with it

steps.title: Download and install
steps.text: Get the .dmg, .msi, .deb or .rpm for your system from runkiri.com/releases. The first time you open Kiri it sets up a `kiri` Docker context.

steps.title: Run a first container
steps.code: docker --context kiri run --rm alpine echo hello

steps.title: Bring your old setup over
steps.text: This imports images, volumes and containers from OrbStack or Docker Desktop.

steps.title: Start Kubernetes if you need it
steps.text: A single-node cluster, set up as the `kiri` kubectl context.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Run `kiri bench` to repeat the project's own speed test on your machine.

watch: Kiri updates itself. It checks each new release's signature first.
It runs its own Linux VM with a custom kernel. The VM sleeps after 60 seconds idle.
The built-in builder is still on the roadmap, so buildx does not yet use its docker driver against Kiri.

items.name: sand3d
items.works_with: Python, Blender's bpy, any AI model you give the API doc to
items.short: A Python library for writing 3D objects as short programs that an AI model can write and a person can read.
items.what: sand3d lets you describe 3D objects as short programs of named parts, edits and joints, on top of Blender's `bpy`. The whole API fits in about 3,600 tokens, so you can put it in a model's prompt. It exports GLB, URDF, USD, IFC, OBJ and STL.
items.who: People who want an AI model to build 3D models, robots or assemblies as code, and Python users who like CAD as code. If you are on Python 3.12, you will need to switch versions first.
needs: On an Intel Mac, Python 3.11, because bpy 5.2 has no wheel there

steps.title: Install it
steps.text: Blender comes with it as the `bpy` module.
steps.code: pip install sand3d        # or, in a uv project: uv add sand3d

steps.title: Write a first program
steps.text: This makes a bracket and exports it. Units are millimetres by default.
steps.code:
import sand3d as s3d

def bracket(w=80, d=40, t=6, hole_d=6.6, pitch=50):
    plate = s3d.extrude("plate", s3d.rect(w, d, r=4), t)
    s3d.hole(plate, hole_d, on=s3d.grid(2, 1, pitch, 0))
    s3d.fillet(plate, 1, edges="top")
    return plate

s3d.export(bracket(), "bracket.glb")

steps.title: Give it to your AI
steps.text: Put `docs/api.md` from the repo in the system prompt. For objects with several parts, the project's guidelines page gives the rules for an assembly program.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Run the bracket program, then change the export to `bracket.stl` or `bracket.obj`. The file extension picks the format.

watch: `bpy` has no wheel for Python 3.12, nor for Intel Macs from 5.2 on. Use Python 3.11 there.
IFC export uses the current pose without joints, and its IDs can change when you edit a part, so do not use them to track parts.

items.name: Chrome DevTools for agents
items.works_with: Any MCP client, such as Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and Gemini CLI
items.short: An MCP server and CLI that let your coding agent control a live Chrome browser for debugging, automation and performance checks.
items.what: chrome-devtools-mcp gives your coding agent Chrome DevTools. It can record performance traces, read network requests and console messages, take screenshots and automate pages through Puppeteer. It also comes as a `chrome-devtools` CLI and with skills that teach your agent how to use it.
items.who: Web developers who want their agent to see what the page is doing in a real browser. It officially supports only Google Chrome and Chrome for Testing.
needs: Chrome, current stable version or newer

steps.title: Add it to your MCP client
steps.text: Add this to your MCP client's config. The README links a guide for each editor and agent.

steps.title: Or install it as a plugin in Claude Code
steps.text: This installs the MCP server and all the skills. Run the second command after the first.

steps.title: Or install it in Gemini CLI
Use the CLI without MCP
steps.code:
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
chrome-devtools navigate_page 1 --url "https://developers.chrome.com"
chrome-devtools take_screenshot 1 --filePath screenshot.png
chrome-devtools stop

watch: Your agent can inspect, debug and change any data in that browser. Do not share anything there you would not want the agent to see.
Google collects usage statistics by default. Opt out with the `--no-usage-statistics` flag.
Performance tools may send trace URLs to Google's CrUX API. Turn that off with `--no-performance-crux`.
It checks npm for updates. Set `CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_UPDATE_CHECKS` to stop that.
Update the skills each time you update the server, or they may describe tools that changed.

items.name: Stitch Design Skills
items.works_with: Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode (manual install)
items.short: Google's AI skills and plugins for the Stitch MCP server: generate screens, extract design systems and turn designs into code.
items.what: A set of AI skills for Google Stitch, in three plugins. stitch-design creates and edits screens and moves designs between code and Stitch. stitch-build turns designs into React, React Native, shadcn/ui and Remotion code, and stitch-utilities helps with prompts and design specs.
items.who: People who already use Google Stitch, or want to, and work in a coding agent. Without the Stitch MCP server set up, these skills will not work.
needs: The Stitch MCP server set up and running in your agent, with its credentials and environment variables (see the Stitch MCP setup guide)

steps.title: Set up Stitch MCP first
steps.text: Follow the Stitch MCP setup instructions at stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/mcp/setup to register the server and set its credentials.

steps.title: Install in Claude Code
steps.text: This installs into the current project.
steps.code: npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope project --target claude-code

steps.title: Install in Cursor
steps.text: This installs into the current workspace.
steps.code: npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope workspace --target cursor

steps.title: Install in Codex
steps.text: Add the marketplace, then install stitch-design, stitch-build or stitch-utilities. The sparse flags are optional and only make the clone faster.
steps.code:
codex plugin marketplace add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --ref main \
  --sparse .agents/plugins \
  --sparse plugins/stitch-design \
  --sparse plugins/stitch-build \
  --sparse plugins/stitch-utilities

steps.title: Or pick single skills
steps.text: The skills often depend on each other, so include what they need.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Make a browse tab for a mobile app for romance and date night ideas.

watch: Every skill needs the Stitch MCP server and its credentials.
Skills installed one by one can break if you leave out the ones they depend on.
OpenCode needs a manual install, and skills with `stitch::` names must be renamed before OpenCode loads them.
The README says this is not an officially supported Google product.

items.name: SkillEvaluator
items.cost: Static checks need no API key. Model and sandbox use can cost money; NVIDIA Build gives eligible members free prototyping
items.works_with: Claude Code, Codex and other agents (as a skill), GitHub and GitLab CI
items.short: NVIDIA's tool for checking AI skills: quality and safety checks, overlap checks, and live runs with and without a skill.
items.what: SkillEvaluator tests AI agent skills in three tiers. Tier 1 checks a skill is safe and well formed, Tier 2 looks for repeated or overlapping guidance, and Tier 3 runs a real agent with and without the skill to see if it helps. You can use it as a CLI, in CI or as a skill in your agent.
items.who: People who write or publish AI skills and want evidence they work. If you only use other people's skills, you probably do not need it.
needs: Python 3.12, 3.13 or 3.14, or uv and Git for the quickstart
An LLM provider key, such as an NVIDIA Build API key, for the model-backed checks
A supported agent and a sandbox (Docker by default) for Tier 3 live runs

steps.title: Check a skill with no API key
Or add it to your repo's CI
steps.text: Run this in a GitHub repository. It opens a setup pull request.

steps.title: Or give it to your agent as a skill
steps.text: Then ask your agent whether your skill is any good, and it runs the CLI.

steps.title: Run all three tiers
steps.text: Only after you have set up a provider, the scanners and an agent sandbox.
steps.code:
uv run --python 3.13 --extra all skillevaluator doctor --env-mode docker
uv run --python 3.13 --extra all skillevaluator validate ./my-skill

watch: The rubric check sends your skill's documentation to the model provider.
Model and managed sandbox use can incur charges.
Tier 1 downloads the SkillSpector and Gitleaks scanners when they are missing, and the project installs other third-party software. Check their licences.
Support is experimental and best effort, with no SLA.
